title: Annual scientific production
what: Number of corpus documents per publication year, stacked by the sub-literature each record was assigned to.
how: Counts of PY in the screened corpus; sub-literature = first inclusion rule matched (see search-protocol.md).
caution: Growth partly reflects database growth and the search design (recent records are better indexed); the last year is incomplete.

title: Average citations per year
what: Mean OpenAlex citation count of documents published in each year, divided by the years since publication.
how: TC = OpenAlex cited_by_count at the pull date; citable years = current year - PY + 1.
caution: Years with few documents (small points) are dominated by one or two highly cited papers; do not read them as trends.

title: Most relevant sources
what: The 20 journals, book series or repositories contributing most documents to the corpus.
how: Counts of the OpenAlex primary-location source. Records with no source recorded are listed in the table but left out of the plot.
caution: Preprint servers (arXiv, SSRN, NBER) rank high because working papers are counted as documents; this is not a journal-quality ranking.

title: Bradford's law
what: Sources ranked by number of documents (log rank); the shaded zone is Bradford zone 1, the small core of sources that carries about a third of the documents.
how: bibliometrix::bradford() on the source field (SO).
caution: With a multi-disciplinary corpus the 'core' is partly an artefact of which sub-literature has the most records.

title: Source dynamics
what: Cumulative number of corpus documents over time in the six most frequent sources.
how: bibliometrix::sourceGrowth(top = 6, cdf = TRUE).
caution: Small absolute numbers: a difference of two or three papers changes the ordering.

title: Most productive authors
what: Authors with the most documents in the corpus (whole counting).
how: Author names from OpenAlex authorships, reduced to SURNAME + initials.
caution: Name disambiguation is imperfect: common surnames with the same initials can be merged, and one person can be split across spellings.

title: Most cited authors
what: Authors ranked by the total OpenAlex citations received by their documents in this corpus.
how: Sum of TC over each author's corpus documents (full credit to every co-author).
caution: A single famous paper puts all of its co-authors at the top; this is citation to corpus papers only, not career citations.

title: Lotka's law
what: Share of authors who wrote 1, 2, 3 ... corpus documents, against the theoretical inverse-square distribution.
how: bibliometrix::lotka().
caution: A topical corpus truncates each author's output, so nearly everyone appears once; this describes the corpus, not the authors' careers.

title: Author production over time
what: For the 12 most productive authors: when their corpus documents appeared (point size = number of documents, shade = citations per year).
how: bibliometrix::authorProdOverTime(k = 12).
caution: Shows only documents that passed this corpus's inclusion rules.

title: Most relevant affiliations
what: Institutions appearing on the most corpus documents.
how: OpenAlex institution of each authorship; one count per document per institution.
caution: OpenAlex affiliation data are missing for many older, book and Indian-journal records, so institutions from well-indexed countries are over-represented.

title: Most relevant countries
what: Countries of author institutions, counted once per document.
how: OpenAlex authorship country codes.
caution: Counts where the authors work, not which country a study is about; records without affiliation data are excluded.

title: Corresponding author's country
what: Documents by country of the corresponding (else first) author, split into single-country and multi-country papers.
how: OpenAlex is_corresponding flag, falling back to the first author; MCP = authors from more than one country.
caution: The corresponding-author flag is missing for many records, in which case the first author is used.

title: Country production and collaboration map
what: Shading = documents with an author in the country (log scale); red arcs = pairs of countries that co-authored, thicker = more joint documents.
how: Author countries from OpenAlex, joined to the 'maps' world polygons; arcs join country bounding-box centres.
caution: Grey means no author affiliation recorded, not no research; affiliation coverage is weakest for India-published and legal sources.

title: Most globally cited documents
what: Corpus documents with the highest total citation counts in OpenAlex.
how: OpenAlex cited_by_count at the pull date.
caution: Global citations reward age and breadth: a highly cited paper may be cited mostly for reasons unrelated to this topic.

title: Most locally cited documents
what: Corpus documents cited most often by other corpus documents - the papers this literature itself treats as central.
how: Exact matching of OpenAlex referenced_works ids between corpus records (not string matching).
caution: Only as complete as OpenAlex reference lists: books, working papers and many Indian and legal journals have no machine-readable references.

title: Most locally cited references
what: The 25 works cited by the largest number of corpus documents, whether or not they are themselves in the corpus.
how: Counts over OpenAlex referenced_works of all corpus records, resolved to metadata by single-record lookups.
caution: Grey bars are intellectual foundations outside the search rules (methods papers, classics); they are context, not part of the topical corpus.

title: Reference publication year spectroscopy
what: How many of the corpus's cited references were published in each year; peaks in the red line mark years with unusually influential older works.
how: Publication years of all resolved cited references (one count per citing document); deviation from a centred 5-year median, as in bibliometrix::rpys().
caution: Covers only references OpenAlex could link to a work record; pre-1950 and non-journal references are under-counted, so absent early peaks are not evidence of absence.

title: Most frequent keywords
what: The 30 keywords attached to the most corpus documents.
how: OpenAlex 'keywords' field (DE); frequency = number of documents.
caution: Keywords are OpenAlex's algorithmically assigned keywords (OpenAlex does not carry author keywords); they reflect OpenAlex's vocabulary as much as the authors' own wording.

title: Keyword word cloud
what: The 120 most frequent keywords, sized by number of documents.
how: wordcloud::wordcloud on OpenAlex keywords.
caution: Word clouds exaggerate long words and hide relationships; use the frequency table for any number. Keywords are OpenAlex's algorithmically assigned keywords (OpenAlex does not carry author keywords); they reflect OpenAlex's vocabulary as much as the authors' own wording.

title: Keyword treemap
what: Share of the 50 most frequent keywords; tile area is proportional to the number of documents.
how: treemapify on OpenAlex keywords.
caution: Keywords are OpenAlex's algorithmically assigned keywords (OpenAlex does not carry author keywords); they reflect OpenAlex's vocabulary as much as the authors' own wording.

title: Trend topics
what: Each keyword is placed at the median publication year of the documents using it (bar = first to third quartile; point size = frequency).
how: bibliometrix::fieldByYear(field = 'DE', n.items = 4 per year).
caution: A late median year can simply mean OpenAlex started assigning that keyword recently; it is not proof that the idea is new.

title: Keyword co-occurrence network
what: Which keywords are attached to the same documents: clusters approximate the sub-topics of the literature.
how: bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(co-occurrences, OpenAlex keywords), top 50 keywords, association-strength normalisation, Louvain clustering, Fruchterman-Reingold layout.
caution: Layout distances are not a metric and change with the random seed; clusters depend on the 50-keyword cut-off.

title: Thematic map
what: Keyword clusters placed by centrality (links to other clusters: how important the theme is to the field) and density (internal links: how developed it is). Quadrants: motor (upper right), niche (upper left), basic (lower right), emerging or declining (lower left).
how: bibliometrix::thematicMap(field = 'DE', n = 250, Louvain); bubble size = keyword occurrences in the cluster.
caution: Quadrant positions are relative ranks within this corpus only and shift with minfreq; a 'niche' theme here may be a large field elsewhere.

title: Thematic evolution (interactive Sankey)
what: How keyword clusters in one period flow into clusters of the next. Time slices cut after: 2011, 2019. PNG maps of each slice are saved alongside.
how: bibliometrix::thematicEvolution(field = 'DE', n = 250) with tercile cut points; flows weighted by the inclusion index.
caution: Cut years were chosen mechanically (terciles of publication years); moving them changes the flows, and early slices have few documents.

title: Co-citation network of references
what: Cited works that corpus documents cite together: clusters are the intellectual bases the literature draws on.
how: bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(co-citation, references) on WoS-style reference strings built from OpenAlex referenced_works; top 50 references, Louvain clusters.
caution: Reflects only records with machine-readable reference lists; economics and information-science journals dominate because they are best indexed.

title: Co-citation network of sources
what: Journals that are cited together, showing which disciplines the literature combines.
how: bibliometrix::metaTagExtraction(CR_SO) then biblioNetwork(co-citation, sources); top 40 sources.
caution: Generic labels such as BOOK or PREPRINT are pooled categories, not single outlets.

title: Bibliographic coupling
what: Corpus documents linked when they cite the same references: groups of papers working from the same prior literature.
how: bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(coupling, references); the 60 documents with the longest reference lists; Salton normalisation; Louvain clusters.
caution: Selecting by reference-list length favours reviews and long articles; documents with no indexed references cannot appear.

title: Historiograph (direct citation network)
what: Chronological map of who cites whom among the 25 most locally cited corpus documents; arrows run from the cited to the citing paper along the time axis.
how: bibliometrix::histNetwork(min.citations = 1) and histPlot(n = 25). A Python version built from exact OpenAlex ids is in py_citation_network.html and py_main_path.png.
caution: bibliometrix matches citations by DOI/label strings, so a few links can be missed; compare with the exact-id Python network.

title: Author collaboration network
what: Co-authorship among the 50 most productive authors.
how: bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(collaboration, authors); association normalisation; Louvain clusters; isolates removed.
caution: Most authors appear once in a topical corpus, so this shows a few teams, not the field's whole social structure.

title: Institution collaboration network
what: Which institutions co-author within the corpus.
how: bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(collaboration, universities) on OpenAlex institutions.
caution: Limited to records with affiliation data; multi-campus systems may appear as separate nodes.

title: Country collaboration network
what: International co-authorship links between the 30 most productive countries.
how: bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(collaboration, countries).
caution: Based on author addresses only; says nothing about which countries are studied.

title: Three-field plot: country - keyword - source
what: Interactive Sankey linking author countries (left), keywords (middle) and sources (right). Saved as HTML because plotly cannot be rendered to PNG headlessly on this machine.
how: bibliometrix::threeFieldsPlot(fields = AU_CO, DE, SO; top 12/15/12).
caution: Only the top items of each field are shown; flows are counts of co-appearance, not causal links.

title: Three-field plot: cited reference - author - keyword
what: Interactive Sankey linking the most cited references (left), the most productive authors (middle) and keywords (right).
how: bibliometrix::threeFieldsPlot(fields = CR, AU, DE; top 12 each).
caution: Top-12 cut-offs hide most of the corpus; use it to spot schools of thought, not to count.
